extracted.intended_audience: Catholic faithful / readers of a catechism (laity, parents, confessor-guided penitents)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical catechetical instructions and obligations for Catholics: moral duties (truth, restitution, purity, charity), Church precepts (Mass, fasting, confession, Eucharist, support of pastors, marriage rules), and preparation for judgment. Provides behavioural standards, definitions, and examples for compliance and reparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restitution of ill-gotten goods
rubrics_metrics.description: We are bound to restore ill-gotten goods, or the value of them, as far as we are able.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restore the article or its value to the rightful owner, or to his children/others who have a right to his goods; if no rightful person can be found, give it to the poor only when the owner cannot be found or reached. Do not substitute giving to the poor when you can restore to the owner. If the stolen article is lost or destroyed, give the owner its value. You need not personally announce the theft when restoring unless the owner already knows; prompt restitution is required—delaying restitution after being able to restore is sinful and may affect sacramental disposition. If you cannot restore immediately, you must have a firm and serious resolution to restore as soon as possible; good intention suffices temporarily but must be sincere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repair unjust damage
rubrics_metrics.description: We are bound to repair the damage we have unjustly caused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any unjust injury or damage done to another must be repaired to the extent one is able; reparations are part of moral obligation and necessary for forgiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighth Commandment — speak truth and protect reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eighth Commandment: Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbor. It commands us to speak the truth in all things and to be careful of the honor and reputation of everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a grave wrong to 'steal' a person's good name; injuring reputation is more serious since it cannot be fully restored. Even true faults should not be told except when necessary or for the good of the person or others. Definitions given: detraction (exposing real faults), calumny (accusing of things not done), slander (malicious circulation). When you have injured character by lying, you must acknowledge the falsehood to those you told and compensate for any losses caused; if what you told was true but harmed the person, at every opportunity say good of him before those you harmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions under the Eighth: rash judgment, backbiting, slander, lies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Eighth Commandment forbids all rash judgments, backbiting, slanders, and lies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rash judgment = believing a person guilty without reason or evidence. Backbiting = speaking evil of persons behind their backs. Never listen to or repeat a backbiter or slanderer; carrying gossip or others' evil words to the person about whom they are said is sinful and causes further evils (anger, hatred, revenge). Revealing entrusted secrets or reading another's letters without consent is dishonest and akin to theft; such acts can be criminal and are dishonorable. Avoid actions that create disputes by passing on evil reports; Scripture condemns 'whisperers.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reparation for lying that injures character
rubrics_metrics.description: They who have lied about their neighbor and seriously injured his character must repair the injury done as far as they are able, otherwise they will not be forgiven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restitution for reputational harm includes public acknowledgement of the falsehood to those to whom it was told and compensation for losses (e.g., job loss) caused by the lie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth Commandment — purity of thought and desire
rubrics_metrics.description: The Ninth Commandment: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's wife; it commands us to keep ourselves pure in thought and desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The command forbids unchaste thoughts, desires of another's spouse, and all unlawful impure thoughts and desires. Impure thoughts and desires are sins unless they displease us and we make effort to banish them promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenth Commandment — avoid covetousness; be content
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tenth Commandment: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's goods; by it we are commanded to be content with what we have and to rejoice in our neighbor's welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covet means inordinate or unlawful longing; desiring another's goods through wrongful means (including wishing harm for acquisition) is forbidden. Legitimate desire to obtain goods by just means (purchase, lawful acquisition) is not covetousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precept: Hear Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: To hear Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation is a chief commandment of the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not hearing Mass on a Sunday or holy day of obligation is a mortal sin unless excused for a serious reason (sickness, care of the sick, imminent danger of death, etc.). Those who have others under their charge (parents, employers) who prevent attendance may be guilty as well. Be punctual and respectful—arrive a few minutes before Mass, avoid habitual lateness (sit in the rear if late), and do not use fatigue or inconvenience as frivolous excuses. Employers should make reasonable arrangements to allow employees to attend Mass on Sundays/holy days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precept: Fast and abstain on appointed days
rubrics_metrics.description: To fast and abstain on the days appointed is a chief commandment of the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional fasting: one full meal (may include meat) plus two smaller meatless meals that together do not equal the full meal; no eating between meals; beverages like coffee and tea permitted (milk/juice/soft drinks noted but seen as mitigating fast). Presently Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are prescribed for fasting (also days of abstinence). Exemptions from fasting include those under 21 or 60 and older (begun 60th year), and those whose infirmity, condition or occupation makes fasting impossible or dangerous. On fast-days observe quantity and kind of food; on abstinence days (Fridays in Lent and other prescribed days) avoid flesh-meat but may eat usual amounts otherwise. Consult confessor if unsure about exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of fasting and abstinence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church commands us to fast and abstain in order that we may mortify our passions and satisfy for our sins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fasting is a form of bodily penance aimed to keep the body under control because the body often leads one into sin. Observance of fasting and abstinence is a primary and efficacious form of penance; even where particular rules have been relaxed, the season (Lent) remains a time of penance and personal choice in practice does not excuse all penance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precept: Confess at least once a year
rubrics_metrics.description: To confess at least once a year is a command of the Church; one is obliged, under pain of mortal sin, to go to confession within the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Within the year’ means the interval between confessions should not exceed a year (or the period between the beginning of one Eastertime and the end of the next). Frequent confession is recommended for spiritual growth and grace to resist temptation; saints sometimes confessed very frequently. Children should go to confession when they are of the age of reason (commonly ~7). Even if one has not knowingly committed mortal sin, frequent confession aids holiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precept: Receive Holy Eucharist during Easter time
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the Holy Eucharist during the Easter time is a commandment of the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to receive Communion during Easter time is a mortal sin. In the country referenced, Easter time runs from the first Sunday of Lent to Trinity Sunday inclusive (15 weeks). One must receive Communion sometime during these weeks to fulfill the precept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precept: Contribute to the support of pastors and Church works
rubrics_metrics.description: We are obliged to contribute to the support of our pastors, and to bear our share in the expenses of the Church and school and any charitable institution connected with the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed amount is assigned by the New Law, but Christians are to give according to generosity; offerings are an act of worship and gratitude to God. The example of tithes/first-fruits is used to teach generosity; withholding from God may bring spiritual consequences. Almsgiving to the poor is considered as given to Christ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage precepts — prohibitions and formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church commands: not to marry persons who are not Catholics, or who are related within the third degree of kindred, nor privately without witnesses, nor to solemnize marriage at forbidden times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaning of third degree: brother/sister = first degree; first cousins = second degree; second cousins = third degree; persons in second cousin relationship or nearer cannot marry without a dispensation. The Church may dispense from its own laws (not from God's law). Catholics must not attempt to marry outside the Church (historical penalties noted); marriages without priestly blessing or witnesses are forbidden. Marriages during Lent and Advent should not be celebrated with pomp or nuptial Mass; quiet weddings may be permitted depending on diocesan laws. The nuptial Mass is preferred as showing reverence and bringing blessings; preparation (confession, Eucharist) is expected. Mixed marriages have limited ceremonial forms and are discouraged; priests' liturgical actions in such cases are restricted to indicate displeasure with disobedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church vs State laws regarding marriage and conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse marriage laws of the Church with those of the State; when the State makes laws contrary to the laws of God or of the Church, one cannot obey such state laws without committing grievous sin; when State laws concern only civil effects (property, inheritance) and are not opposed to God's or Church law, they may be obeyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil legal technicalities that free you legally do not necessarily free you in conscience from obligations; a civil court decision in an unjust suit does not justify keeping what was obtained fraudulently in conscience. Obedience to lawful civil authority is required except where it conflicts with divine/Church law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holy days and the divine office for clergy
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy days were instituted to recall the great mysteries of religion and the virtues and rewards of the saints; priests and bishops must say the divine office every day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The divine office is the prayer of the universal Church (prayers, hymns, lessons, psalms) and differs by day; neglecting to say the divine office is a mortal sin for clergy. Lay faithful should keep holy days as they keep Sundays to recall and honor mysteries and saints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper conduct and preparation for Mass and sacraments
rubrics_metrics.description: To hear Mass properly one should be in place a few minutes before the priest, make an intention or ask a blessing; conduct, dress, and demeanor at sacraments must reflect dignity and holiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating sacramental events as mere social amusements; prepare spiritually (confession, prayer) and externally (modest dress, reverent behavior). Habitual lateness, distraction, or treating Mass as a social event displays disrespect and may endanger sacramental fruit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular and General Judgment — preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ will judge us immediately after death (Particular Judgment) and again on the last day (General Judgment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for judgment by daily examen of conscience, acts of contrition, resolutions to avoid sin, prayer, and good works. The Particular Judgment occurs at the moment of death when the soul perceives its state; the General Judgment will publicly reveal all deeds. Cultivate acquaintance with Christ and holiness so that judgment will be welcomed rather than feared.
